title: Lumbar spinal stenosis
intro: Lumbar spinal stenosis is a narrowing of the spinal canal in the lower back that puts pressure on nerves. It typically affects older adults and causes leg pain, tingling or weakness when standing or walking, which eases when sitting or bending forward. Many people improve with exercise and conservative care, and surgery is an option for severe cases.

sections.heading: Causes
paragraphs: With age, discs lose height and bulge, joints enlarge, ligaments thicken and bone spurs form. Together these reduce the space for the nerves. Previous injury, spinal slippage and being born with a narrow canal also contribute. Changes on scans are common in people without symptoms.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: The characteristic symptom is pain, heaviness, numbness or weakness in the buttocks and legs that comes on with walking or prolonged standing and eases with sitting, leaning forward or bending, for example leaning on a shopping trolley. Back pain may be present. Walking distance shortens over time.

sections.heading: Warning signs
paragraphs: Seek urgent medical help for sudden weakness in the legs, numbness around the genitals or buttocks, or loss of control of the bladder or bowels, which can signal severe nerve compression requiring emergency treatment.

sections.heading: Non-surgical treatment
paragraphs: Staying active matters. Physiotherapy with flexion-based exercises, stretching and strengthening of core and leg muscles, walking aids, and cycling, which is usually comfortable because the spine is bent forward, are helpful. Painkillers may ease symptoms. Epidural injections of corticosteroid can give temporary relief but benefits are limited.

sections.heading: Surgery
paragraphs: Decompression surgery removes bone and tissue that press on nerves, sometimes with fusion of vertebrae for instability. It tends to improve leg pain and walking distance in people who have not improved with conservative treatment, but carries risks such as infection, nerve injury and repeat surgery, and results vary. The decision depends on symptoms, ability to walk, other health conditions and preference.

examples.title: Using the shopping trolley
examples.text: Imagine you can walk longer when leaning on a trolley. You could mention this to your doctor, as it helps characterise the problem, and ask about walking aids or exercise.

examples.title: Weighing surgery
examples.text: Suppose you can only walk fifty metres before leg pain forces you to stop. You might ask a spinal surgeon about benefits, risks and recovery, and compare these with continuing with exercise.
